log: WHAT 4D CHROMATIN WOULD COST -- multiplied out from what was actually measured here
chr1 249 Mbp -> 1.2 M nucleosomes | genome 3.1 Gbp -> 15.5 M nucleosomes  (at 200 bp repeat)
WALL 1 -- MEMORY. The atomistic route, priced from the measured sparsity.
measured: 4,870,395 nonzeros over 13,625 atoms = 357 per atom
one nucleosome       13.6 katoms       4.9 Mnonzeros       58.4 MB for the Hessian alone
chr1                 17.0 Gatoms       6.1 Tnonzeros       72.8 TB for the Hessian alone
genome              211.2 Gatoms      75.5 Tnonzeros      905.9 TB for the Hessian alone
Chromosome-scale atomistics is not slow, it is impossible: the matrix does not fit, and
no amount of waiting changes that. This is why the route below is coarse-grained.
WALL 2 -- TIMESTEP. A twistable worm-like chain, one bead per nucleosome, integrated.
4 degrees of freedom per bead (position + twist), 200 flops per bead-step (ESTIMATE)
chr1       memory    39.8 MB | 0.1 s/step | transcribing one 10 kb gene takes 303 s biological
= 30.3 Gsteps at dt=1e-08 s -> 59.8 years of compute
genome     memory   496.0 MB | 0.8 s/step | transcribing one 10 kb gene takes 303 s biological
= 30.3 Gsteps at dt=1e-08 s -> 744.7 years of compute
Memory is now trivial and the wall has MOVED, not gone. Integration pays for every
1e-08 s whether anything happened or not, and biology runs on seconds.
WALL 3 -- OR NOT A WALL. Stop integrating. The measured relaxation spectrum says why.
Chromatin is overdamped (Reynolds ~1e-9) and this repo measured its relaxation times
spanning tau 7.2 to 48794 within a single nucleosome. A polymerase adds
one base every 30 ms. If elastic re-equilibration is fast against that --
and overdamped relaxation is -- then nothing is gained by resolving the interval. The
scheme becomes: advance to the next EVENT, re-solve the static problem, repeat.
That is exactly the closed-form solver already built here, used as a stepper.
AND THE PER-EVENT COST IS NOT A FULL RE-SOLVE, which is the whole point of the two-level
machinery. Priced at the iteration level instead, because that is what the solver does:
matvec        2 x nnz, with ~256 nonzeros per bead (bonded, bending, twist, excluded volume)
coarse        2 x DOF x 200 modes -- project, solve a diagonal, prolong
local solves  one small dense solve per sphere, ~one matvec in total at the measured H^1.2
A COLD solve took 64 two-level iterations here. A polymerase step perturbs a few
hundred base pairs and the previous state is an excellent initial guess, so a WARM restart
should need far fewer -- 5 is assumed below and is the softest number in this file.
scenario                             events  per event        warm        cold
transcribe one 10 kb gene, 10 bp/event    1.0 k      4.1 s       1.1 h      14.5 h
transcribe 1,000 genes concurrently    1.0 M      4.1 s   47.3 days   1.7 years
one replication fork, 1 kb/event, chr1  249.0 k      4.1 s   11.8 days  150.6 days
full S phase, genome, 1 kb/event      3.1 M     50.8 s   5.0 years  64.0 years
on 4 cores. These divide by cores almost exactly -- every operation above is a
matvec or a dense projection, both of which parallelise without communication headaches.
On 256 cores the S-phase row falls to 28.5 days.
ADAPTIVE REFINEMENT -- coarse everywhere, fine only where it is needed
coarse 10 kb   dt  21.85 us   1.39e+07 steps
fine   200 bp  dt   8.74 ns   3.47e+10 steps   (1.36 persistence lengths)
THE DOMAIN IS ALMOST FREE. 10 kb fine window, multiple time stepping:
domain          coarse beads    4 cores   256 cores
100 kb                     9   1.0 days    22.6 min

A 2,490-fold increase in domain costs 20% more, because the coarse level is nothing.
IT IS ENTIRELY THE FINE WINDOW, and that is linear in window size:
window          fine beads    4 cores   256 cores
2 kb                    10      4.8 h     4.5 min
10 kb                   50   1.0 days    22.6 min
MULTIPLE TIME STEPPING IS NOT OPTIONAL. With one global dt, refining anywhere forces the
fine timestep EVERYWHERE and most of the saving evaporates:
uniform 200 bp everywhere          100.3 days      100x
refine the window, one global dt     3.0 days      3.0x
refine the window + MTS              1.0 days      1.0x
SEQUENTIAL REFINEMENT -- coarse for the full time, then break the beads down
The modes that appear on halving a bead have tau between tau(b) and 4 tau(b), so they
equilibrate in ~20 tau(b) at dt = tau(b)/10: about 200 steps per level, at every level.
level      bead         dt    sim time     steps   beads  bead-steps
L0      10000bp  21.8515us        303s  13867684     100    1.39e+09  FULL biological time
TOTAL 1.39e+09 bead-steps = 1.2 min for 1 Mb on 4 cores
The coarse level is 99.8% of that; all six refinements together add 0.16%.
Against uniform 200 bp for the whole 303 s: 100.3 days, a 124798x difference.
WHAT IT ACTUALLY BUYS, and this is the whole caveat. Sequential refinement gives an
EQUILIBRATED FINE SNAPSHOT, not a fine TRAJECTORY. It is legitimate because the fine
modes are slaved to the coarse ones -- tau(200 bp) = 87 ns against tau(10 kb) = 219 us,
a factor of ~2,500 -- so the fine structure is a FUNCTION of the coarse state and can be
regenerated on demand rather than carried.
It breaks precisely when that stops being true:
HYSTERESIS   a plectoneme pinned at a sequence feature, a bubble that stays open. Then
the fine state depends on history, not on the current coarse state.
FEEDBACK     a melted segment has C ~ 0 and ssDNA bending stiffness, which changes the
COARSE rod's mechanics. Tier 1B is exactly this case, so denaturation
cannot be a post-hoc refinement -- it has to run inside the loop wherever
melting is possible.
So the practical scheme is both: sequential refinement everywhere for conformation and
topology, and a persistent fine window only where melting or polymerase activity lives.
THE ENGINEERING RISK, and it is one thing rather than many. Splitting a 10 kb bead into
fifty 200 bp beads and merging them back must conserve LINKING NUMBER EXACTLY. Lk is the
quantity the whole model exists to track, it is topological rather than energetic, and a
small leak at a moving refinement boundary will not show up as an instability -- it will
show up as slowly drifting supercoiling that looks like physics. Lk conservation across
every refine and coarsen operation should be an assertion, not a hope.
What is NOT a risk: the stiffness mapping. A persistence length is scale-free, so the
discrete bending stiffness is just A/b at any level. Atomistic coarse-graining has no such
luxury, and this is the one place the rod model is genuinely easier.
THE ASSUMPTION THAT CARRIES ALL OF IT, stated so it can be attacked.
Quasi-static stepping is only valid if the structure re-equilibrates BETWEEN events. The
slowest mode measured here is tau_max = 48794 in the solver's units, and those units
are not seconds -- gamma was never calibrated to water. THAT CALIBRATION IS THE ONE
MISSING NUMBER, and it decides whether this whole scheme is legitimate or a fiction.
It is a small measurement (fit one mode's relaxation against a known diffusion
coefficient) and it should be done before any of the costs above are quoted as real.
READING
Atomistic chromosome: ruled out on memory, permanently.
Coarse-grained + integration: possible in principle, decades of compute, ruled out in practice.
Coarse-grained + EVENT stepping: hours to days on hardware we have, because the cost stops
scaling with simulated TIME and starts scaling with the number of things that HAPPEN.
Twist and polymerase fit that scheme directly. Replication fits it as a topology edit between
solves. Denaturation does NOT -- it is a bond-breaking event the harmonic model cannot
represent at any cost, and needs a base-pair free-energy layer instead of more compute.
